questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a reform can be reversed even when its original rationale was sound
questions.stem: A transit authority abandoned a district-level permit scheme two years after introducing it. Explain in one paragraph why a reform can be reversed even when its original rationale was sound.

answer.exemplar: A reform can be reversed without its original rationale being wrong, because the reasoning that justified the change does not by itself secure political support for it. The district scheme was defensible on efficiency grounds, yet it shifted visible costs onto small operators and removed discretion that local managers valued. Once those costs were felt and the benefits remained hard to observe, the coalition that backed the reform weakened, and the organisation reverted to an arrangement it knew well. Reversal is therefore usually a problem of coalition maintenance and visibility rather than of analytical error.

questions.explanation: A sound rationale secures the decision, not its survival; reversals usually reflect coalition and cost-visibility problems rather than bad analysis. The paragraph should name those political conditions.
questions.hint: Separate the reasoning from the support.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how sequencing changes the risk carried by a reform programme
questions.stem: A transport authority merged eleven depots in three waves and wants to explain why the order mattered. Explain how sequencing changes the risk of a reform programme.

answer.exemplar: Sequencing determines what each stage depends on and therefore how failure propagates. In the depot merger, the first wave rebuilt supervision structures in three depots; the second and third waves then moved staff into those structures. Had the payroll transfer preceded the supervision redesign, managers would have inherited staff without the new reporting lines and the payroll error would have been invisible until the audit. A sound sequence places the structural change before the transaction that depends on it, so that failure is detected while it is still cheap to correct. Sequencing also protects political consent, because each stage delivers visible results before the next stage asks for disruption.

questions.explanation: A good answer connects sequence to dependency: each stage must build the structure the next stage relies on, or errors surface late at higher cost. It should also note that visible early results build consent for later disruption.
questions.hint: Ask what each stage depended on.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a shared definition enables coordination between agencies
questions.stem: Two agencies that both inspect bus shelters publish separate reports with different definitions of a safe shelter. Explain how a shared definition would improve coordination.

answer.exemplar: Coordination fails here because each agency measures the same thing differently, so neither report can be read against the other and duplicated or missed repairs go unnoticed. Agreeing a single definition of a safe shelter, together with the inspection evidence that satisfies it, creates a common object that both agencies are accountable for. Shared definitions also make trend data comparable across years and districts, which is what allows scarce repair funds to be directed at the shelters with the worst measured condition. Without the shared definition, each agency can improve its own score while the network as a whole stays unrepaired in the same places.

questions.explanation: A strong answer explains that agencies cannot coordinate when they measure the same thing differently, and that a shared definition creates a common object both are accountable for and makes trend comparisons meaningful.
questions.hint: Consider what happens without one definition.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how decentralisation produces uneven service and what it costs
questions.stem: Districts with the same resources deliver visibly different bus services. Explain how decentralisation can produce variation, and what it costs.

answer.exemplar: Decentralisation moves operational authority to district offices, and each office develops its own working assumptions, staff habits and relationships with local operators. Where central oversight is thin, the same rules produce different service quality in different places, which is efficient in the sense that local knowledge is used but expensive in the sense that citizens in one district get a worse deal than citizens in another. The cost is borne unevenly, since residents cannot easily see or compare the standard they receive against that of a neighbouring district. Central standards, common definitions and published comparison are the usual means of limiting that variation without removing local discretion.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that local discretion produces legitimate variation but also unequal citizen experience, especially where central oversight is thin, and identifies common standards and published comparison as the usual check.
questions.hint: Consider what residents in each district receive.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why publication alone does not produce accountability
questions.stem: A transport authority published its budget and the board wants to explain why disclosure alone does not guarantee accountability. Write a short account.

answer.exemplar: Disclosure supplies the record, not the scrutiny. Publication gives citizens, journalists and councillors a common factual basis for asking questions, but three things must be added before published figures change anyone's behaviour: the figures have to be complete enough to cover the decisions that matter, there must be some body obliged to answer questions about them, and the answers have to be connected to a consequence such as a budget revision or a service change. Where a budget is published without explanation of its link to service outcomes, readers can see that money was spent but cannot tell whether it was spent well, and officials who spend badly face no specific penalty for having done so.

questions.explanation: A good answer argues that publication provides a shared factual basis for scrutiny, but accountability also needs coverage, a duty to answer and consequences for bad answers, none of which publication creates by itself.
questions.hint: Distinguish the record from the scrutiny.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Set out how a league table should be built so that it survives definitional disputes
questions.stem: Districts dispute a published league table because the measure of reliability is defined differently in each district. Explain how a board should build a league table that survives such disputes.

answer.exemplar: A league table that districts dispute on definitional grounds will be disputed again, so the board has to fix the definition before it ranks anything. The measure has to be written so that two officials working independently would classify the same service the same way, and the definition should be published together with the decision on how unusual cases are treated, such as a journey cancelled after the first stop. The frame of comparison matters too: the same service must be counted for every district over the same period, and any change to the frame must be recalculated for earlier years rather than silently applied. Then the table should carry the underlying figures so a district can check the arithmetic rather than argue about the method. Finally, a place should be reserved for the cases the measure cannot capture, since a district serving a remote area or a heavily disrupted line will always look worse on a punctuality figure, and a board that publishes no adjustment invites a permanent argument that the adjustment is a favour.

questions.explanation: A strong answer should require a published written definition applied identically, a fixed comparison frame with recalculation when it changes, published underlying figures, and a stated treatment of cases the measure cannot capture.
questions.hint: Fix the definition before the ranking.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Pay linked to activity and to outcome
questions.learningObjective: Explain why adding a bonus component failed to change a behaviour
questions.stem: A depot pays drivers a bonus for completed journeys and for punctual departures, but drivers now leave late-running routes until the delay clears. Explain why adding a punctuality bonus failed to fix the behaviour.

answer.exemplar: The bonus scheme rewarded two things at once, the number of journeys completed and the number that departed on time, and the problem arose from the interaction between them. A driver who waits for a late route loses a departure, but the wait also improves the punctuality of the journey that finally starts, so the two components pull in opposite directions on the same behaviour. Where the value of an on-time journey is high enough, waiting becomes rational: the driver recovers more by waiting than by starting on time and hoping to catch up. Adding a punctuality component did not help because it strengthened the same reward that already made waiting attractive, rather than changing what waiting costs. The remedy is structural rather than financial: punctuality has to be measured across the shift rather than per journey, so that a departure made on time by waiting for a late route counts as a recovery rather than as an achievement, and the loss falls on the trip that was never made.

questions.explanation: A strong answer should show that the two bonus components pull in opposite directions on the same behaviour, that waiting raises the punctuality of the next journey, and that the fix is to measure punctuality across a shift.
questions.hint: Ask what a waiting driver gains.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a target can be satisfied on paper while service deteriorates
questions.stem: Explain how a performance target can be met on paper while service quality on the ground deteriorates.

answer.exemplar: A target defines a measurement, and anyone who can satisfy the measurement without satisfying the underlying purpose will do so, because the target is what gets monitored and rewarded. Four forms of this are common in transport. Selecting: the operator chooses the journeys, routes or days that get inspected, so the sample flatters performance. Timing: services are scheduled so that measured journeys avoid the difficult periods. Definition: a journey counts as punctual under a rule that treats a departure as on time even when the previous bus has gone, so bunching disappears from the figures while passengers still feel it. And reporting: the operator sets the baseline, the measure and the period, so improvement is claimed against a weak comparison. The remedy is independent measurement with published definitions, sampling that the operator cannot choose, and comparison against a fixed standard rather than a self-selected baseline.

questions.explanation: A good answer separates satisfying the measure from achieving the purpose, giving mechanisms like self-selected samples and weak baselines, then naming independent measurement as the fix.
questions.hint: Ask what the target cannot see.

The busier district has better management than the other
options.misconception: reduces a structural difference to managerial quality

options.text: The difference cannot be explained without knowing passenger numbers
options.misconception: insists on a factor that does not explain service levels

questions.explanation: Such differences usually arise where a common funding rule meets different local conditions, such as route length or road space. The tempting readings assume identical conditions or blame competence.
questions.hint: Ask what the districts share.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Choose the arrangement that ends duplicated responsibility for one place
questions.stem: A region reviews bus shelters and a separate agency reviews the pavement around them, and each repairs only its own object. Which arrangement best avoids duplicated work?

options.text: Ask both agencies to inspect the same locations in the same month
options.misconception: synchronises inspection without joining the responsibility

options.text: Require the agencies to swap inspection reports every quarter
options.misconception: shares information but keeps the split responsibility

options.text: Give one agency responsibility for the whole location, including the pavement
Ask a third agency to check that both have done their inspections
options.misconception: adds oversight rather than removing duplication

questions.explanation: Duplicated work arises from splitting one place between two responsibilities, so one agency owning the whole location removes the overlap. Synchronised inspections, shared reports and a third checker do not.
questions.hint: Ask who owns the whole location.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read a sequence of results as evidence about how changes interact
questions.stem: A board introduced a shared booking system, then merged customer service teams, then changed the timetable. Complaints fell after each step. What does the sequence of results suggest?

options.text: Each step caused the fall in complaints on its own
options.misconception: attributes the whole improvement to any single step

options.text: Later steps benefited from the foundations the earlier steps created
The order of the steps was unimportant because each produced a fall
options.misconception: ignores that later steps depended on earlier ones

options.text: The fall in complaints was caused by something outside the programme
options.misconception: invents an external cause the results do not show

questions.explanation: Complaints fell after each step, which fits a sequence where each stage built what the next needed. The other readings credit one step for everything or deny the sequence any role.
questions.hint: Ask what each stage made possible.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a reform loses the political support that enabled it
questions.stem: Explain, for a transport board, how a reform can lose the political support that made it possible.

answer.exemplar: Support for a reform rests on a coalition that forms when the change is made and dissolves as its consequences arrive. Three things commonly dissolve it. Costs become visible and concentrated while benefits stay diffuse and delayed, so the people who bear the cost make more noise than the people who gain. Second, responsibility blurs: once the reform is operating, its failures are attributed to the people running it rather than to the decision to start, which converts an advocate into a target for blame. Third, attention moves. A new crisis, an election or a rival scheme gives opponents a moment when inaction is cheaper than defence. Boards that expect reversal treat these as design questions, staggering benefits so early wins are visible, and keeping decision ownership separate from operational ownership so that failure is not read as personal disgrace.

questions.explanation: A good answer should show that support is a coalition of interests, and that it dissolves through visible concentrated costs, blurred responsibility or shifting attention, then link that to design choices boards can make.
questions.hint: Ask who loses and who notices.
